C005.subject: Remote work
C005.object: collaborative, interdependent tasks requiring real-time coordination
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work collaborative, interdependent tasks requiring real-time coordination]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing task completion time and error rates for collaborative software development teams working remotely vs. co-located on time-sensitive, interdependent tasks (e.g., debugging a live system). — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring individual efficiency under real-time coordination demands, controlling for confounding variables like task complexity and communication medium.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on remote work productivity, focusing on studies that isolate task interdependence and real-time coordination (e.g., papers indexed in PsycINFO or Web of Science using keywords: 'remote work', 'task interdependence', 'real-time coordination', 'efficiency'). — Aggregates existing evidence across multiple contexts to assess the generalizability of the hypothesis and identify moderators (e.g., team size, communication tools).

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of digital trace data from collaboration platforms (e.g., Slack, Jira, GitHub) measuring individual throughput and response latency on tasks with high dependency chains before and during the pandemic. — Provides objective, high-resolution behavioral data to quantify efficiency changes in real-world settings, complementing self-report measures and addressing the temporal scope of the hypothesis.

C006.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work solitary, deep-focus tasks]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing task completion times and error rates for solitary deep-focus tasks (e.g., coding, writing) between remote and co-located knowledge workers, using time-tracking and output quality metrics. — Direct causal evidence on individual efficiency can be obtained by isolating the remote work condition while controlling for task type, interruptions, and environmental factors, addressing the disputed status with high internal validity.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on remote work productivity (e.g., from journals like Journal of Applied Psychology or Management Science) focusing specifically on solitary, cognitively demanding tasks, with moderator analysis for task complexity and autonomy. — Synthesizing prior evidence can reveal consistent patterns or heterogeneity across studies, helping to confirm or refute the hypothesis while accounting for publication bias and varying operational definitions of 'deep-focus tasks'.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey and diary study tracking knowledge workers' self-reported deep-focus time, flow states, and task completion rates over several months, with pre- and post-remote work transition comparisons. — Capturing temporal dynamics and within-subject changes can address the post-2020 surge context, providing ecological validity and insights into adaptation effects that cross-sectional designs miss.

C007.subject: Remote work
C007.object: complex collaborative projects that require high-frequency, unstructured communication
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work complex collaborative projects that require high-frequency, unstructured communication]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study comparing communication logs (e.g., Slack, email, meeting transcripts) between co-located and remote teams working on complex R&D projects, measuring coordination breakdowns (e.g., response delays, misalignment episodes) and project outcomes (e.g., time-to-decision, innovation quality). — Directly tests the predicate by quantifying coordination effectiveness in high-frequency, unstructured communication contexts, controlling for project complexity and team size.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of published experiments and surveys on remote collaboration (e.g., from journals like Organization Science or Journal of Applied Psychology) focusing on moderating variables such as task interdependence, communication modality richness, and team familiarity. — Aggregates existing evidence to assess whether the effect is robust across studies and identifies boundary conditions (e.g., whether video calls mitigate the reduction).

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling team coordination under varying remote work conditions (e.g., asynchronous vs. synchronous communication, network topology) to predict emergent coordination failures in complex, high-stakes projects. — Provides a causal mechanism explanation for how remote work disrupts spontaneous information sharing and rapid feedback loops, allowing counterfactual testing of alternative coordination structures.

qualifier.temporal: since the widespread adoption of remote work in 2020

C008.subject: Remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote work complex collaborative projects]

[PATH:empirical] A meta-analysis of field experiments comparing remote vs. co-located teams on complex innovation tasks (e.g., product design or strategic decision-making), controlling for task interdependence and communication frequency. — Directly tests the causal claim by aggregating high-quality experimental evidence across contexts, addressing the disputed status with quantitative synthesis.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal case studies of global software development or R&D teams (since 2020) that measure coordination effectiveness via objective metrics (e.g., project milestones met, error rates, rework time) and subjective team surveys. — Provides contextualized, real-world data on remote coordination in complex, collaborative projects, capturing temporal and geographic scope while controlling for confounding factors like team maturity.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of media richness and task complexity applied to remote work (e.g., updated Daft & Lengel framework), tested with simulation or archival data from project management tools. — Explains the mechanisms (e.g., information loss, synchronicity) that might enhance or hinder coordination, offering a falsifiable basis for the hypothesis and guiding empirical design.

C011.subject: Office work
C011.object: mentoring of junior employees from underrepresented backgrounds
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Office work mentoring of junior employees from underrepresented backgrounds]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study comparing mentoring outcomes (e.g., career advancement, retention, satisfaction) for junior employees from underrepresented backgrounds in office vs. remote settings, controlling for industry and company size (e.g., data from LinkedIn, internal HR records). — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring whether in-person interaction provides unique benefits for mentoring of underrepresented groups, such as informal networking and sponsorship, which may be harder to replicate remotely.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on remote work and equity in professional development, focusing on mentoring of underrepresented groups (e.g., studies from journals like Journal of Vocational Behavior or Harvard Business Review). — Synthesizes available evidence to determine if patterns across studies support or contradict the hypothesis, accounting for contextual factors like industry, mentorship structure, and demographic composition.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from social capital theory and organizational behavior, examining how physical co-location affects trust-building, informal knowledge transfer, and psychological safety for underrepresented mentees. — Provides a causal mechanism to explain why office work might outperform remote work in this context, or identifies conditions (e.g., structured virtual mentoring programs) that could mitigate any disadvantage.
